sections.html:
Carpentersville is a village in northern Kane County on the Fox River. The 2020 census counted 37,983 residents in 8.09 square miles, up 0.8 percent from 37,691 in 2010. Carpentersville handles its own permits, water billing and rental licensing, so most of the paperwork stays at Village Hall instead of moving to a county office.

The 2020 census recorded 11,777 housing units, 2.9 percent of them vacant, with a homeowner vacancy rate of 0.9 percent and a rental vacancy rate of 5.0 percent. A rate that low suggests few for-sale houses sit empty, which helps a seller who prices sensibly. Median household income is $73,105, so many buyers will need a mortgage. That is one reason some owners prefer a cash buyer who does not depend on lender approval.

sections.h2: Older river blocks and newer subdivisions
sections.html:
The village has two kinds of housing. The older street grid along the river centers on Main Street, and the population jumped from 1,523 in 1950 to 17,424 in 1960 as subdivisions arrived. Newer subdivisions and shopping centers have gone up west along Randall Road since the 1990s.

Know which type you own before you price. Younger families make up much of the village, with a median age of 32.5 in 2020, so house size and layout matter to the likely buyer pool. If your house is in the older river-side grid, ask Village Hall whether any local review applies before you plan exterior changes.

Carpentersville has no transfer stamp requirement for real estate transactions, which makes it one of the simpler closings in the northwest suburbs.

The seller still has one task. Call the Water Billing Department at 847-551-3476 to schedule a final reading on the water meter. The new owner then opens service in person at Village Hall with a settlement statement or deed, a completed water application and picture identification.

State tax still applies. Illinois taxes the transfer of title at 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction thereof under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, based on the declaration filed for the sale.

The Community Development Department issues permits for construction, and even a new water heater or a shed needs some kind of permit or approval. The village links a list of work that does and does not need one.

  • Past work: if the previous owner added a deck, finished a basement or replaced a furnace, confirm the permit was closed.
  • Open work: a buyer who takes the house as-is takes the open permit with it.
  • Rental houses: the village runs a rental licensing program with an initial inspection and an annual license.

The rental licensing steps start with a temporary certificate after an application, then an inspection, then a follow-up inspection if violations are found, and a Crime Free Housing seminar the owner must attend. Ask Community Development for the current version of the checklist before you rely on it.

If you plan to sell a tenant-occupied house, remember that the owner is responsible for getting tenant consent for inspection visits.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Kane County
sections.html:
The Kane County Recorder in Geneva keeps the land records for the village. The recorder's website offers a records search, and the office provides recording, copying, scanning and a tract department.

The recorder also runs a free Property Watch service aimed at deed fraud, which targets homeowners at risk of foreclosure. An owner of a vacant or inherited house may want to look at it.

Water is the only village item that every Carpentersville seller must schedule. Call Water Billing as soon as you have a closing date, and ask for the final reading to match that date. Keep the final bill with your closing papers so the title company can see it was settled.

The new owner has to show up in person at Village Hall, so tell your buyer about it early. They bring the settlement statement or deed, a completed water application and picture identification. A buyer who learns this the day of closing may lose a day or two before service is in their name.

With no village stamp, closing in Carpentersville comes down to the title company, the state declaration and the deed. The declaration sets the state tax at 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction thereof. After signing, the deed goes to the Kane County Recorder in Geneva, which records it and adds it to the land records.

Ask your title company for a settlement statement before the closing date and read each line. A cash purchase usually closes faster because no lender has to approve the buyer, though the same paperwork applies. Keep a copy of the deed and the statement for your own records.

A listing makes sense when the house is move-in ready and you can wait out showings and a buyer's financing. A cash sale as-is makes sense when repairs, a tenant, an inherited estate or a deadline would make a listing slow or costly.

Either way the village side is light: no municipal stamp, a final water reading and the permit review above. That leaves your time and repair costs as the real variables, so compare the net result of each route and not just the headline price.

sections.h2: Steps to take before you list
sections.html:
Start with the permit question, because it can take the longest to answer. Ask Community Development about any deck, basement, furnace or water heater work done since the house was built. Next, call Water Billing and set the final meter reading. Then gather the deed or settlement statement for the new owner's water application, and tell your title company which county recorder will file the deed.

If the house is a rental, ask about the license status and the inspection history, and tell the tenant about any inspection visit. A buyer who plans to keep the tenant will want to see the lease and the license together.

sections.h2: What a cash buyer will ask
sections.html: Expect questions about the roof, the furnace, the basement and any open permits. A cash buyer pricing a house as-is counts those items against the offer, so having permit papers and repair receipts on hand can lift the number. Ask the buyer to confirm in writing who pays for the water reading, any open permit work and the recording step.

faqs.q: Do I need a village transfer stamp to sell in Carpentersville?
faqs.a: No. The village has no transfer stamp requirement for real estate sales. You should still schedule a final water meter reading by calling Water Billing at 847-551-3476.

faqs.q: What does the buyer need to start water service?
faqs.a: The new owner brings a settlement statement or deed to Village Hall in person, fills out the water application and shows picture identification.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed for a water heater or shed in Carpentersville?
faqs.a: In general, yes. Work from a new water heater or shed up to a full building requires some type of permit or approval. Check the village's list of work that does and does not need a permit before you start.
Kane County. The Kane County Recorder in Geneva records deeds and offers an online records search.

faqs.q: How much did Carpentersville grow in the last census decade?
faqs.a: Slightly. The population rose from 37,691 in 2010 to 37,983 in 2020, a gain of 0.8 percent.
